extracted.intended_audience: grant writers and administrators at educational institutions; faculty and staff preparing external grant proposals
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for selecting funding sources and preparing competitive grant proposals for institutional programs (chiefly education/higher-education). Covers pre-application research, proposal structure, content, budgeting, review, submission, and follow-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand funding organizations' program plans
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations and agencies that award grant funds do so according to master program plans. Funding plans typically will project goals, objectives, and funding allocations for one or more years into the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review public announcements, brochures, and program materials to learn an organization's purpose, structure, funding priorities, proposal requirements, schedule and award amounts. Match your proposed work to their projected goals and priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request and review the grant application package
rubrics_metrics.description: Contact each funding organization and request their grant application package; materials usually describe the organization's purpose, structure, funding priorities, proposal requirements and procedures, schedule and amount of awards, and special instructions and forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully read all application materials and follow prescribed forms and special instructions. If questions remain, use letter or telephone contact with a program representative to clarify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine fit and applicant eligibility before applying
rubrics_metrics.description: When contacting a potential funding source, first determine if your application will fit their priorities and if your institution is an eligible applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm eligibility and fit early to avoid wasted effort. If initial response is favorable, proceed to more detailed questions about requirements, deadlines, and award structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask specific pre-application questions of the funder
rubrics_metrics.description: Explore key questions with a funder’s representative about whether your request meets goals, whether a preliminary proposal is needed, award size and number, partial awards, past funded applicants, strengthening features (matching funds), and cyclical deadlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a checklist of questions: Who is the appropriate contact? Will request meet next cycle goals? Preliminary concept paper required? Total funding available, award size, number planned? Are partial awards made? Will funder share prior awardees? What special features strengthen an application? What are deadlines?

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain additional printed materials and annual reports
rubrics_metrics.description: If additional printed materials are available from the organization, request a copy for review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain program policy statements, annual reports, guidelines, and application forms to better understand priorities, timelines, and submission requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact previous applicants for insights and sample proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: Contact previous grant applicants (winners and losers) for insights about their requests and ask for a copy of their proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review successful and unsuccessful proposals to learn what worked and common pitfalls. Ask targeted questions to past applicants about application procedures and reviewer expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicit advice from colleagues and community contacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Contact individuals in other organizations or colleges, charitable body members, school boards, state and federal representatives (or their staff), and local civic/business leaders to explore willingness to help and to learn about funders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage institutional and community networks for intel, endorsements, or introductions; people who write/read proposals often have useful advice even for different funders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select promising funding sources before preparing proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: First select the most promising sources of funding, then contact each organization and request their application package; after reviewing the application information, resolve questions about match and eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do targeted applications only to funders whose priorities align with your project and where you meet eligibility—this increases chances of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think like the reviewer — key reviewer questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Experienced proposal writers view submissions from the funding organization's perspective by asking: Is the main idea clearly and logically presented? Does the project merit the amount requested? What distinguishes the proposed program? Is content and style impressive? Are assurances given that the funds will be spent wisely?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these reviewer questions as a litmus test while drafting: clarity, cost-justification, distinctiveness, presentation quality, and fiscal assurances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow the funder's requested format exactly
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow the format requested by the funding agency or copy the format used in previous successful proposals. Be sure to include all required pieces and do not include extraneous or expensive-looking brochures or enclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to follow format or inclusion of inappropriate enclosures can send the wrong message and hurt competitiveness. When in doubt, follow the funder's instructions precisely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write objectives as measurable, outcome-focused statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Write the program objectives in terms of measurable results that reflect important outcomes for students, faculty, the institution, and/or the community at large.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think of results that would make good newspaper stories; present objectives in concise bulleted statements that focus on important, measurable outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain how funds will enable objectives (budget-activities linkage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare a careful explanation of how the requested funds will enable your program to meet the program objectives. Funding organizations look for assurances that funds will result in positive outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly link budget items to activities and outcomes; show logical causality between funds expended and results achieved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use clear, concise, non-obscure language
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the use of obscure language and convoluted writing. Good proposals are clear, the key ideas are presented concisely, and the narrative is understandable to laypersons as well as experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try to state the key concept in one sentence. Make the narrative accessible to non-specialist reviewers without sacrificing necessary technical detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain focus and avoid overly-complex or multiple alternative approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: If your proposal offers overly complex or too many alternative approaches, it may be judged as overly-technical or lacking in focus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present a coherent, focused plan rather than many divergent options. Clearly justify chosen approach and avoid confusing reviewers with too many contingencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate confidence and avoid hedging language
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempt to demonstrate confidence in the approach, ideas, and outcomes. Avoid broadcasting self-doubt with 'ifs' and 'buts' and 'maybes'. State what will be done and, when in doubt, do not propose risky ventures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use positive, assertive phrasing to convey feasibility and preparedness; limit speculative or high-risk proposals unless funder seeks innovation with risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use data and reliable evidence to support need and plans
rubrics_metrics.description: Data, especially in the form of numbers and graphs, help make a strong case. Data should come from reliable sources and present or support needs, timetables, specific evaluation plans, and so forth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include cost-per-student calculations or multi-year cost analyses to highlight return on investment. Source data and cite references; include charts/graphs for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate broader value and external support
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong proposals show the readers that the outcomes to be achieved will be of value to more than one group and include evidence that the program is supported by others, especially external to your institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include letters of support, evidence of volunteer support, advisory panel endorsements, and documentation of in-kind contributions from businesses or civic organizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid requesting funds for regularly-budgeted activities or for proven inadequate programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Good proposals do not ask for funds for programs that should be getting regular funding from within your system nor do they ask for money to conduct a program that has been tried and proven inadequate by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funders expect proposals for innovative or pilot activities, capacity-building, or clearly justified needs—not to supplant routine internal funding or revive failed models without substantial justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include sincere recognition opportunities for the funder
rubrics_metrics.description: Where practical, try to include some sincere form of recognition of the funder (e.g., named facility, plaque, invitations to events, publicity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor recognition to funder type (corporate, foundation, individual) and be genuine—these strategies can encourage giving and strengthen relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invest in personal contact and relationship-building with funders
rubrics_metrics.description: Funding decisions are sometimes made independent of the proposal process; funders provide funds to individuals and groups they know and trust, regardless of the quality of proposals from unknown applicants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain personal contact, build respect and trust with funder representatives, and use relationships to complement the proposal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a proposal development sign-off schedule and backward planning
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposal development sign-off schedule should list the title, essential funding information, names of writers and reviewers, and critical steps (writing, reviewing, typing, sign-off, mailing) with sign-off spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan backward from mailing date, allow extra time for delays (busy schedules, reviewer changes, budget revisions), and share the timeline with everyone involved, including clerical staff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include required title page elements
rubrics_metrics.description: A title page may contain the proposal title, funding organization name, principal investigator's name, project time span, amount requested, and date of submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check institution or funder for preferred format. A separate signature page may simplify layout when required by the funder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write a concise abstract (150–300 words) and draft it early
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose, activities, and outcomes of the proposed project should be described in 150 to 300 words in the abstract. It is helpful to write a preliminary draft of the abstract before the full proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the abstract to clarify key ideas and serve as a standard against which later changes are judged; review and revise the abstract after the full proposal is completed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a Background subsection in the Introduction showing institutional capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Background should present important information about the proposing institution—mission, situation, previous similar projects, size, number of students served, measures of effectiveness, relationships, and past uses of funds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate capacity to carry out the project by summarizing relevant past successes and institutional strengths with supporting facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft a strong Statement of Problem/Need with supporting data
rubrics_metrics.description: The Statement of the Problem should describe the need to be addressed with the funds; reviewers may retain or eliminate proposals on the basis of this section during early review cycles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present concise summary of compiled needs-analysis data (include supporting data in appendix), explain costs of not resolving the problem, and summarize expected benefits to convince reviewers early.

rubrics_metrics.name: State Project Objectives clearly and prominently
rubrics_metrics.description: The Project Objectives subsection presents the specific intended outcomes of the proposed project or activity and should highlight the factor of most interest to the sponsor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use bulleted, possibly bold-typed objective statements that are hard-hitting, solid, and clearly tied to sponsor interests (target populations, industry/career fields, economic goals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Detail Plan of Action with phases, activities, and tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: The Plan of Action section should present detailed procedures and activities; list major steps or phases and then break into tasks, numbering each item so order and relationships are clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide overview (Activities), then Tasks with numbered hierarchy (Phase 1.0, Activity 1.1, Task 1.1.1, etc.), and ensure task numbers correspond to the time line schedule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a clear Project Time Line
rubrics_metrics.description: The Time Line subsection should include a calendar of events with notes, placing lines/symbols to show when each part of the work begins and ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the phase/activity/task outline to construct a schedule (e.g., Gantt chart). Include sample time line in appendices for reviewer clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe staff roles, responsibilities, time commitments, and qualifications
rubrics_metrics.description: The Staff Section provides information on staff who will work on the project, including roles, responsibilities, and qualifications. A table may show time per month each person will spend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Name persons when possible and summarize qualifications; include a staff matrix to show percent effort and ensure key positions are filled or will be filled if funded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe facilities and include supporting drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: The Facilities Section describes the buildings, labs, classrooms, etc., in which the program will operate and any features important to carrying out the project; include floor plans or drawings as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight unique or necessary facilities for project success and include visuals to clarify plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a precise, objective-linked Evaluation plan
rubrics_metrics.description: The Evaluation Section describes in detail the methods to be used to evaluate outcomes or success. The evaluation methods and measures should relate directly to the objectives of the project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be very precise about procedures and measures, indicate how degree of success will be measured, and include copies of existing assessment instruments in an appendix where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare a detailed budget with year-by-year breakdown and cost categories
rubrics_metrics.description: The budget section should identify each item of cost separately and may group items into categories such as salaries, equipment, tuition waivers, etc.; for multi-year projects, provide total and year-by-year breakdowns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use institutional standard budget forms if provided. Itemize costs so reviewers can see exactly how funds will be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check and document indirect costs and funder limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect costs for overhead usually are applied as a percentage of direct costs; most funding organizations have limits on indirect costs they will pay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm institution's indirect charge rate with business office and verify the funder's limits before submitting budget; adjust budget to funder policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write a confident Capacity Statement demonstrating ability to conduct the project
rubrics_metrics.description: A capacity statement describes resources and past achievements to show ability to carry out the proposed project; it should make the sponsor proud to be part of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be confident and positive without sounding arrogant; provide supporting data rather than self-congratulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include consistent-format resumes in an appendix
rubrics_metrics.description: Resumes are included to show staff are properly experienced and qualified; they are included as an appendix and should have the same format unless the funder stipulates otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a position will be filled after award, include credentials of the person to be hired. Ensure uniform formatting across resumes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use internal and external reviewers and a reviewer checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: After writing, have the proposal reviewed by individuals within and outside your institution; a reviewer checklist can help focus attention and comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully consider reviewer suggestions and make revisions as appropriate. Do not slavishly follow every suggestion—use reviewers to improve clarity and quality. Acknowledge reviewers and inform them of results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow submission formatting and physical-copy best practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals are usually double-spaced, with left margin 1 1/4 inches and right margin 3/4 inches; number pages for easy reference. Duplicate enough copies and reproduce on good-quality paper; colored cover stock and spiral binding are appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow any funder-specified formatting; prepare multiple clean copies for funder and internal offices; ensure professional appearance but avoid over-expensive enclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mail, track, confirm receipt, and follow up appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Mail copies to the funding organization through registered mail and keep the postal receipt as evidence. After adequate delivery time, call and confirm arrival; be prepared to supply additional information if requested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain an orderly file of project scope documents, capacity evidence, fiscal items, budget justifications, and need documentation to respond promptly to funder inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request evaluative feedback if proposal is not funded
rubrics_metrics.description: In the event your proposal is not funded, request as much evaluative feedback as can be provided to help improve the next attempt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use funder feedback to refine future proposals, address weaknesses identified, and improve competitive positioning.
